# Abstract

Curation — the transformation of raw information into decision-grade knowledge — is the bottleneck behind most coordination failures. Centralized curation predictably fails through incompetence (incentive divergence from knowledge quality) and weaponization (exploiting control over the information-to-knowledge pipeline); generative AI makes this structurally worse by decoupling quality's form from its substance.

We propose a four-step framework for trustless decentralized curation: problem definition, use case selection, quality identification, and mechanism design. Instantiating it for news curation yields two quality dimensions: accuracy (global, binary, dispute-resolved) and relevance (local, non-binary, resolved by a policy-guided coherence game where curators rate conformity to a public curation policy and outliers are slashed). A 2023 partial deployment (Truth Post) tested the accuracy layer only; its failure to bootstrap directly informed the full design.

Adversarial simulations show the dispute mechanism is economically punitive against well-funded attackers, the coherence game ejects colluding minorities but breaks above ~20-30% of stake, and a reputation mechanism accelerates cash-poor expert entry at a quantified equity-accuracy tradeoff. This paper addresses curation only; coordination given shared knowledge is out of scope.

# Introduction

You search for a cafe and your maps app returns a list sorted by ratings. You research a medical question and a search engine ranks the answers. You choose a university and a magazine's ranking steers the decision. You did not produce any of this knowledge; you consumed it. And you had no practical alternative: the cost of independently verifying every input to every decision you make exceeds any individual's capacity. Curation is not a convenience; it is a dependency you cannot opt out of.

To coordinate, people first need a shared picture of reality. That shared picture is produced by **curation** — the transformation of raw information into knowledge. Most hard problems are two-phase: (1) **curation** — converge on what is true and important enough to act on; (2) **coordination** — align actions given that shared knowledge. The thesis of this paper: **the bottleneck is almost always phase one.** We keep trying to fix coordination with better governance and voting while standing on a broken knowledge layer. We propose a framework for trustless decentralized curation and instantiate it for news, where the bottleneck is most visible and the cost of failure most broadly distributed. This paper addresses phase one only; coordination given shared knowledge is out of scope.

In this paper, "knowledge" is used operationally: a claim becomes decision-grade only after it is (a) well-posed, (b) tied to an explicit evidence policy, and (c) contestable under incentives. The protocol outputs are therefore **signals** — not guarantees.

## Information abundance, knowledge scarcity

The internet solved access to *information* but not access to *knowledge*. Information is raw: a claim, a data point, a signal. Knowledge is information that has been verified, contextualized, and integrated into a coherent understanding. The transformation from one to the other is curation. Institutions once performed this transformation through editorial selection, peer review, and pedagogy. Today we have far more information and far weaker mechanisms to convert it.

Generative AI makes this structurally worse. Historically, the cost of producing information served as a crude quality filter: writing a convincing paper required understanding the subject. AI severs that coupling — the *form* of quality (proper formatting, confident language, plausible citations) is now trivially cheap to generate, while the *substance* (correctness, coherence, domain understanding) is not. The volume of information that needs filtering is growing faster than any existing curation process can handle.

## Operationalizing knowledge: from JTB to contestable signals

Traditional epistemology treats knowledge as **justified true belief** (JTB). The protocol operationalizes each component:

| JTB component | Protocol mechanism | Section reference |
|---|---|---|
| **Truth** | Binary accuracy verdict (Valid/Invalid) resolved by DDR under an evidence standard | Flow 3 |
| **Justification** | Evidence bundles with integrity commitments; evidence policies define admissible sources and tie-break rules | Evidence policy; Claim templates |
| **Belief** | Authorship requires stake; a claim is not merely asserted but economically committed to | Flow 1 |

The protocol does not claim to produce truth. It produces **stake-weighted, contestable labels** under an explicit evidence standard. This operationalization inherits Gettier cases [@gettier1963justified] — a claim can be stake-validated and true by coincidence while the supporting evidence is misleading — as a residual risk rather than a solvable problem.

## When common knowledge fails

Coordination often fails because people confuse shared knowledge with common knowledge. In game theory, **common knowledge** [@aumann1976agreeing] requires not just mutual knowledge of $X$ but infinite recursive awareness of that knowledge. Theoretical models suggest humans routinely overestimate the depth of shared knowledge [@bolander2020common], producing an illusion that masks incompatible understanding.

## Why this matters

In domains where decisions allocate real resources, bad curation is a selection pressure against excellence: restaurant rankings that reward mediocrity drive out quality restaurants; university rankings that mismeasure quality redirect students and funding. Users lose in time and decision quality; honest creators lose to sensational work optimized for distribution; trust erodes (global trust in news hovers around 40% [@reuters2024digitalnews]).

When curation is centralized, two failure modes emerge: *incompetence* (the curator's incentives diverge from knowledge quality) and *weaponization* (the curator exploits control over what becomes "known" [-@chomsky1988manufacturing]). The critical insight: these are indistinguishable from the consumer's perspective. This is not a bug in any particular platform; it is an inherent property of centralized curation.

## Contributions

- **A general framework for trustless decentralized curation**: a four-step process (problem definition, use case selection, quality identification, mechanism design). Use case selection requires: (1) publicly verifiable evidence, and (2) falsification substantially cheaper than exhaustive verification. The framework is domain-agnostic; the remaining contributions instantiate it for news curation.
- **A news curation instantiation**: quality decomposition into accuracy (global, binary) and relevance (local, non-binary), with a coherence game for relevance (collusion threshold ~20-30% of stake), security design principles (semantic ambiguity as attack vector; protocol/interface separation), and a public good analysis with parallels to the Groves-Ledyard deviation penalty.
- **An adversarial evaluation**: reproducible simulations covering incentive alignment, coherence dynamics, ambiguity failure modes, repeated economic attacks, and coordinated collusion.
- **A deployment retrospective**: Truth Post (2023) deployed the accuracy layer only; its failure to bootstrap participation directly informed the full design.


# Background and problem statement

## Failure modes of centralized curation

The root structural property is **opacity**: when one entity controls the transformation of information into knowledge, the consumer cannot audit why content was promoted, suppressed, or ranked, and therefore cannot detect systematic error. Opacity enables **capture** (the curator optimizes for its own objectives rather than the consumer's epistemic needs) and **gaming** (external actors optimize against a single mechanism at scale). Unilateral control enables **censorship** and creates **fragility** (the knowledge layer inherits every failure of the curator). Finally, centralized curation offers **no contestability**: errors persist until the curator independently chooses to act.

## Why quality collapses: adverse selection in information markets

Consider two restaurants competing in the same neighborhood. One invests in quality; the other cuts corners. If the curation mechanism ranking them cannot distinguish the two, the cost difference is a pure competitive disadvantage for the quality restaurant. Over time, the quality restaurant must reduce quality or exit — not because consumers prefer inferior food, but because the curation layer failed to make quality visible.

The mechanism is adverse selection [@akerlof1970lemons]: when curation cannot distinguish quality, high-quality producers face higher costs without proportional recognition and exit. This pattern operates in every domain where quality is expensive to produce and difficult to observe: journalism, scientific research, software, education. Centralized curation intensifies rather than corrects this failure: opacity prevents consumers from observing quality, and capture means the curator's incentives favor cheap-to-produce, high-engagement content.

## What good curation must optimize for

When curation drives resource allocation decisions, when consumers cannot independently verify quality, and when the curator's incentives can diverge from the consumer's, the failure modes described in the previous section become inevitable unless the system satisfies specific process properties. Each property addresses a specific failure: **well-posed** claims (falsifiable and unambiguous) prevent disputes from degenerating into semantic games; **auditable** processes (every assertion, verdict, and stake movement publicly traceable) counter opacity; **contestable** outputs (any participant can challenge by posting stake and counter-evidence) counter the absence of correction mechanisms; and **incentive-aligned** mechanisms (correctness is profitable, dishonesty is expensive) counter capture. Without these properties, any system operating in high-stakes, low-verifiability domains will reproduce the same failures under a different name.

**Domain-specific quality criteria (news and information curation).** Applying the framework's quality identification step to news yields three criteria:

1. **Evidence-backed**: tied to an explicit evidence policy defining admissible sources and tie-break rules. Operationalized as the *accuracy* dimension.
2. **Coherent**: consistent with other validated claims in the same domain. Operationalized as the *relevance* dimension.
3. **Current**: truth decays; claims become stale.

A different instantiation (e.g., scientific claims, product reviews) would identify different domain-specific criteria.

To illustrate domain-agnosticism, consider **advertising claim verification.** Applying the four-step framework: the advertiser posts a bond with a structured product claim; if the claim survives the challenge window, the bond is returned (cost approaches zero for truthful claims); if falsified, the advertiser loses the bond. This inverts the cost structure relative to current compliance regimes where costs are fixed regardless of truth value. The advertiser staking mechanism in the Funding section implements this instantiation, which collapses to a single quality dimension (accuracy).

The remainder of this paper develops mechanisms for the news curation instantiation.

Extended data-quality and credibility mappings (Wang & Strong dimensions, CRAAP checklist) are available in [Supplementary Material A](supplementary-material.md).

# System model and assumptions

## Actors

- **Authors** submit claims with evidence bundles and a bounty at risk.
- **Validators** stake on pools, becoming eligible for random drafting into relevance rounds (as curators, Flow 4) or the juror-eligible population for disputes.
- **Challengers** contest claims by posting counter-stake and counter-evidence, triggering dispute resolution.
- **Jurors** are drawn from the DDR system (e.g., Kleros) to adjudicate disputes; they are distinct from validators.
- **Interface operators** build consumer-facing applications; they control UX and compliance but not the underlying record.
- **Governance participants** vote on protocol parameter updates ($\alpha$, $K$, pool creation rules).

## Artifacts: claims, evidence, verdicts

The unit of curation is a **claim**: a single proposition + scope (timeframe, definitions, jurisdiction) + resolution policy + selected pool. Each claim has an **evidence bundle** (public references + integrity hashes) and receives a **verdict**: Valid / Invalid / Under-specified. Under-specified means the claim cannot be adjudicated because required information is missing or ambiguous; ambiguity is a failure, not something jurors should guess.

## Evidence policy

Each pool publishes an **evidence policy** specifying accepted evidence types, canonical sources, tie-break rules, and thresholds for Valid vs Under-specified. Jurors adjudicate *policy compliance* rather than inventing semantics mid-dispute.

## Trust assumptions

This design does not eliminate trust; it **constrains** it. We treat dispute resolution as a **black box DDR system** (e.g., Kleros) requiring only: (1) stake-weighted random juror selection, (2) Valid/Invalid/Under-specified verdicts, and (3) appeals with escalating stakes. Evidence authenticity is imperfect and must be contested, not assumed.

# Mechanisms

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $B$ ($B_t$) | Bounty posted by the claim author (at interval $t$) |
| $S$ | Challenge stake posted by a challenger |
| $C$ | Confidence score: $C = \sum_t B_t \cdot \Delta t$ |
| $v_i$ | Curator $i$'s relevance rating, $v_i \in [0, 1]$ |
| $w_i$ | Curator $i$'s vote weight: $w_i = s_i + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{rep}_i$ |
| $s_i$ | Curator $i$'s financial stake |
| $\mathrm{rep}_i$ | Curator $i$'s non-transferable reputation (topic-scoped) |
| $\alpha$ | Pool parameter: reputation-to-weight conversion factor |
| $\mu$ | Weighted mean of relevance ratings |
| $\sigma$ | Weighted standard deviation of relevance ratings |
| $K$ | Coherence threshold: curator $i$ is coherent iff $|v_i - \mu| \le K\sigma$ |
| $R$ | Optional protocol reward added to the coherence game pot |
| $N$ | Jury size (odd integer) |
| $p$ | Per-juror correctness probability |
| $d$ ($p_{\text{detect}}$) | Probability a false claim is detected and challenged |
| $n$ | Number of curators drafted for a relevance round |
| $\mathcal{V}$ | Strategy space (report domain): $\{\text{Valid}, \text{Invalid}\}$ for DDR, $[0,1]$ for coherence game |
| $v^*$ | Focal point: the honest assessment of policy conformity |
| $u_i$ | Payoff function for player $i$ |
| $P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N)$ | Majority-correct probability for $N$ jurors with per-juror accuracy $p$ |
| $GF$ | Griefing factor: $\text{harm}_{\text{victim}} / \text{cost}_{\text{attacker}}$ |

: Key notation used throughout. {#tbl-notation}

## Overview: separation of powers

The quality identification step identifies two dimensions that centralized platforms conflate into engagement:

- **Accuracy**: global, binary classification under an evidence standard, resolved via dispute processes.
- **Relevance**: local, non-binary importance produced by a policy-guided coherence game.

Accuracy is global because a factual claim is valid or invalid regardless of who reads it. Relevance is local because importance depends on context, curation policy, and moment. A different domain would decompose quality differently (e.g., reproducibility for science, admissibility for legal evidence).

## Formal model: Schelling coordination under restricted conditions

Both the accuracy dispute (Flow 3) and the relevance coherence game (Flow 4) are Schelling coordination games: agents submit simultaneous reports under commit-reveal, and payoffs reward agreement. @george2023strategic proves an impossibility theorem: for three or more ranked alternatives, truthful reporting cannot always be an equilibrium. Our contribution is to identify **restricted conditions** under which truthful reporting *is* a Nash equilibrium.

### Base game

A Schelling coordination game $\Gamma$ consists of:

- **Players**: $n$ agents drawn from a pool, each with weight $w_i$.
- **Strategy space**: each player simultaneously submits a report $v_i \in \mathcal{V}$.
- **Simultaneity enforcement**: commit-reveal prevents observation of others' reports before commitment.
- **Payoff function** $u_i(v_i, v_{-i})$: coherent players (those whose reports fall within a threshold of the aggregate) share the pot (slashed stakes from incoherent players, plus an optional protocol reward $R$); incoherent players lose stake proportionally.

The "coherent" predicate is parameterized by the game instantiation. The griefing factor framework [@george2023griefing] provides a formal measure of attack cost: the griefing factor $GF = \text{harm}_{\text{victim}} / \text{cost}_{\text{attacker}}$ bounds how much damage an adversary can inflict per unit of self-cost. A mechanism with $GF \le 1$ ensures that attacking costs the adversary at least as much as it costs the victim.

### Instantiation 1: binary accuracy (DDR disputes)

The dispute mechanism (Flow 3) instantiates $\Gamma$ with $\mathcal{V} = \{\text{Valid}, \text{Invalid}\}$. Under-specified is a structural rejection (template validation failure), not a ranked alternative — so George's impossibility does not apply. The DDR mechanism exploits the asymmetry between falsification and verification: it is justified for claims where falsification is cheap (a counterexample suffices) but exhaustive verification is expensive. The claim must be falsifiable not merely in principle but at a cost rational given the bounty.

For the $S/B$ ratios tested in E1 (0.05 to 0.50), the break-even majority threshold ranges from 0.048 to 0.333, all exceeded when $p > 0.50$ with $N = 5$. The binding requirement is $p > 0.50$: each juror must be better than random for the incentive structure to be self-enforcing.

The griefing factor for a challenger attacking a true claim is $GF = \frac{B \cdot P_{\mathrm{maj}}}{S \cdot (1 - P_{\mathrm{maj}})}$. At $p = 0.80$ and $S/B = 0.25$, $GF \approx 37$: the attacker pays far more than the victim. For a legitimate challenger, the asymmetry is reversed — the intended incentive.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 1 (Condorcet connection)"}
If per-juror accuracy $p > 0.50$ and votes are independent, the majority-correct probability $P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N) = \sum_{k=\lceil N/2 \rceil}^{N} \binom{N}{k} p^k (1-p)^{N-k}$ is monotone increasing in jury size $N$ and converges to 1 as $N \to \infty$. Challenger expected value is positive whenever $P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N) > \frac{S/B}{1 + S/B}$.
:::

For the $S/B$ ratios tested in E1 (0.05 to 0.50), the break-even majority threshold ranges from 0.048 to 0.333, all of which are exceeded when $p > 0.50$ with $N = 5$ jurors. The binding system requirement is therefore $p > 0.50$: each juror must be better than random for the incentive structure to be self-enforcing.

For the $S/B$ ratios tested in E1 (0.05 to 0.50), the break-even majority threshold ranges from 0.048 to 0.333, all exceeded when $p > 0.50$ with $N = 5$. The binding requirement is $p > 0.50$: each juror must be better than random for the incentive structure to be self-enforcing.

The griefing factor for a challenger attacking a true claim is $GF = \frac{B \cdot P_{\mathrm{maj}}}{S \cdot (1 - P_{\mathrm{maj}})}$. At $p = 0.80$ and $S/B = 0.25$, $GF \approx 37$: the attacker pays far more than the victim. For a legitimate challenger, the asymmetry is reversed — the intended incentive. For a legitimate challenger disputing a false claim, the asymmetry is reversed, which is the intended incentive.

### Instantiation 2: scalar relevance (coherence game)

The coherence game (Flow 4) instantiates $\Gamma$ with $\mathcal{V} = [0, 1]$ (continuous scalar). Reports are aggregated by weighted mean $\mu$ with a $K\sigma$-threshold coherence rule, not ranked over discrete alternatives. George's impossibility applies to rankings; scalar aggregation with a coherence band is a different game structure where the impossibility does not directly bind.

The focal point is the honest assessment of curation policy conformity: given a specific, public curation policy, the degree to which an item conforms is the unique salient coordination target.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 2 (focal point equilibrium)"}
Under commit-reveal, if (a) the curation policy is specific enough to induce a unique focal point $v^*$, (b) $K$ is large enough that honest noise from competent curators falls within the coherence band with high probability, and (c) no pre-commitment communication channel exists, then all curators reporting $v^* + \epsilon_i$ (honest assessment with individual noise) is a Nash equilibrium. Deviating from the honest assessment increases the probability of falling outside the $K\sigma$ band and incurring slashing.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 3 (competence selection)"}
Under repeated play, agents whose noise variance exceeds the coherence band's tolerance lose expected stake per round; agents within the band gain. The pool's competence composition improves endogenously. This requires $K$ and the slash rate to be set such that expected loss for incoherent participants exceeds expected gain from random coherence.
:::

The equilibrium degrades under identifiable conditions: (a) vague curation policy (weak focal point; condition (a) of Proposition 2 fails), (b) small $n$ (high variance in $\mu$), and (c) extreme competence skew (too few competent curators to anchor the mean). These degradation conditions make the system's governance dependencies explicit and measurable.

## Vagueness = Rejection: claim templates as a security primitive

A jury can only resolve what is specified. Claims must carry enough structure that "correct" is not a matter of vibes: single proposition, explicit scope (time, location, units/definitions), and explicit resolution policy. If missing, the correct verdict is **Under-specified**. Each pool publishes a versioned **claim template** (required fields) and **evidence policy** (admissible evidence, tie-break rules).

### The curation policy bootstrap problem

Writing good curation policies is itself a governance problem. The bootstrapping direction has four components: (1) **start minimal** — pools launch with narrow policies; (2) **policy amendment as dispute** — proposals are subject to the existing dispute mechanism; (3) **forking as safety valve** — participants can fork pools with captured policies; (4) **cross-pool competition** — pools with vague policies produce weak focal points (Proposition 2 degrades), lose participants, and shrink. The equilibrium degrades gracefully, making governance failures measurable through output quality.

### Defending against strategic ambiguity

Allowing Under-specified as an outcome creates a cheap way to reject ambiguous claims, but also introduces adversarial behavior (borderline claims, dispute spam). Mitigations:

- **Ambiguity slashing**: if a claim is ruled Under-specified, the author loses stake (failure, not "close enough").
- **Template linting**: UIs run deterministic checks before acceptance (missing timeframe, missing source class, undefined terms).
- **Policy-defined semantics**: if a domain requires fuzziness, it must define it explicitly (turning semantics into policy compliance).

## Common criticism: "consensus ≠ correctness"

Schelling-style mechanisms maximize *coherence*, not truth directly [@bergolla2022kleros; @kleros2021cryptoeconomics; @rojoarjona2021focalpoints]. This design responds: (1) ill-posed claims are rejected as Under-specified; (2) appeals raise stakes, attracting expertise; (3) jurors adjudicate policy compliance, not metaphysical truth.

## Flow 1: submission and confidence signaling

### Protocol

1. **Claim authoring.** The author selects a pool, drafts a claim conforming to the template, attaches an evidence bundle, and specifies a bounty $B$.
2. **Template validation.** The interface verifies required fields; non-conforming claims are rejected.
3. **Submission.** The author locks $B$ on-chain; the confidence score clock starts.
4. **Confidence accumulation.** $C$ increases by $B_t \cdot \Delta t$ for each uncontested interval.
5. **Outcome (optimistic finality).** If no challenge is filed within the window, the claim is marked Valid by default. This is an explicit design choice — *optimistic finality* — borrowed from optimistic rollup and oracle designs (e.g., UMA [@umaOptimisticOracleDocs]): the system assumes correctness unless someone stakes capital to dispute it. The tradeoff: optimistic finality minimizes latency and cost for honest claims (no jury needed in the common case), but false claims survive whenever challengers are absent or under-capitalized. The confidence score partially compensates: unchallenged claims with low bounty carry low $C$, signaling that absence of challenge is not rigorous validation.

### Confidence score

$$
C = \sum_{t} B_t \cdot \Delta t
$$

The unit is token·time (e.g., ETH·hours), intentionally non-normalized. Within a pool, higher $C$ means more skin-in-the-game-over-time. Cross-pool comparison requires interface-level normalization (e.g., $C_{\text{norm}} = C / \text{median}(C_{\text{pool}})$). $C$ is intentionally non-normalized — it is not a probability and is not comparable across pools with different token denominations. Cross-pool comparison requires interface-level normalization. Invariants: $C$ is monotone during uncontested periods (pauses during challenges, terminates on Invalid/Under-specified) and gated (zero bounty = zero confidence).

## Flow 2: pooled staking (liability and chilling effects)

Validators stake on **pools** (topic-scoped domains) rather than individual claims.

1. **Pool creation.** Governance creates a pool with evidence policy, claim template, and parameters ($K$, $\alpha$, minimum stake).
2. **Staking.** A validator locks stake $s_i$, becoming eligible for random drafting. Withdrawals require a cooldown period.
3. **Random drafting.** The protocol draws from the pool using on-chain randomness (VRF-based), weighted by stake.
4. **Payout/slashing.** Coherent/correct validators earn rewards; incoherent/incorrect validators lose stake.

**Liability diffusion.** Because validators do not choose specific claims, targeted legal pressure (e.g., "you validated claim X, so you are liable for defamation") is diffused across the entire pool. The larger the pool, the weaker the per-validator liability signal, raising the cost of targeted chilling effects substantially.

## Flow 3: challenge, dispute, appeals

1. **Challenge**: any user posts stake $S$ against a claim with bounty $B$, submitting counter-evidence.
2. **Juror selection**: the DDR system draws jurors using on-chain randomness.
3. **Commit phase**: jurors commit vote hashes within the voting window.
4. **Reveal phase**: jurors reveal votes; non-reveals forfeit stake.
5. **Verdict**: majority vote determines the outcome.
6. **Payout**: challenger wins → receives $B + S$ minus fees; challenger loses → author receives $S$.
7. **Appeal**: either party appeals by posting higher stake (e.g., $2\times$ previous), drawing a larger panel. Upper bound: maximum appeal count or cost ceiling $A_{\max}$.

**Economics.** For an individual challenger: $\text{EV}_{\text{challenger}} = P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N) \cdot B - (1 - P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N)) \cdot S$. For the system (including detection): $\text{EV}_{\text{system}} = d \cdot [P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N) \cdot B - (1 - P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p, N)) \cdot S]$, where $d$ is detection probability. These are distinct: a challenger who has found a provably false claim faces only jury risk ($p$), while the system's false-claim suppression depends on both detection coverage ($d$) and jury accuracy ($p$). Challenger EV is positive whenever $p > 0.50$ for all $S/B \le 0.50$; the minimum-$p$ requirement is stated after E1. Juror vote independence is assumed; herding and off-chain coordination are addressed in the threat model.

**Commit-reveal limitations.** Commit-reveal reduces herding but is not an anti-bribery primitive; it cannot prevent off-chain coordination [@consensysPlcrVoting; @consensysDiligenceTcrAudit].

## Flow 4: relevance via coherence game

Relevance is produced by a policy-guided coherence game — a Schelling-point mechanism [@schelling1960strategy]: *to what degree does this item conform to the pool's curation policy?*

### Protocol

1. **Eligibility.** Curators stake $s_i$ on a pool. Staking more increases drafting probability.
2. **Drafting.** The protocol draws $n$ curators using on-chain randomness (VRF-based), weighted by stake.
3. **Commit phase.** Each curator commits $h_i = H(v_i \| \text{salt}_i)$ for rating $v_i \in [0, 1]$, where $v_i$ represents degree of conformity to the curation policy (0 = none, 1 = full).
4. **Reveal phase.** Curators reveal $(v_i, \text{salt}_i)$. The protocol verifies $H(v_i \| \text{salt}_i) = h_i$. Non-reveals forfeit stake.
5. **Aggregation.** Compute weighted mean $\mu = \frac{\sum_i w_i v_i}{\sum_i w_i}$ and weighted standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i w_i (v_i - \mu)^2}{\sum_i w_i}}$.
6. **Coherence rule.** Curator $i$ is *coherent* iff $|v_i - \mu| \le K\sigma$, where $K$ is a pool parameter.
7. **Payout.** Incoherent curators surrender stakes. The pot (slashed stakes + optional protocol reward $R$) is distributed among coherent curators proportional to weight.

### Premature reveal and collusion defense

Commit-reveal prevents observation of others' ratings before committing. Premature reveal (leaking committed values) enables coordination; the defense is report-based slashing. This is acknowledged as an incomplete defense against off-chain coordination.

### Equilibrium argument

Under commit-reveal, the curation policy defines the focal point. Propositions 2 and 3 establish: (a) honest assessment is a Nash equilibrium when the policy is specific enough, $K$ accommodates honest noise, and no pre-commitment channel exists; (b) under repeated play, incompetent curators lose stake and exit, producing endogenous competence filtering. George's impossibility [@george2023strategic] does not bind because the coherence game uses scalar aggregation with a $K\sigma$ threshold, not rankings over discrete alternatives.

### Focal-point uniqueness: scope and limitations

Condition (a) of Proposition 2 assumes the curation policy induces a unique focal point. This is a design heuristic, not a theorem. Multi-modal response distributions arise when raters disagree on attribute definitions. *Sufficient condition*: single-attribute policies with a publicly enumerable value space and unambiguous attribute definitions produce approximately unimodal interpretation distributions. *Counterexample*: "rate journalistic quality" conflates dimensions (source diversity, accuracy, prose clarity) and produces bimodal distributions among honest curators. *Design implication*: policies that satisfy the sufficient condition are the recommended starting point; multi-dimensional policies should be decomposed into constituent dimensions scored separately.

### Whale manipulation risk

A high-weight participant can shift $\mu$ substantially. Mitigations: (a) per-participant weight caps ($w_i \le w_{\max}$), (b) competence filter (incoherent participants lose stake over time).

### Accuracy-relevance interaction

Accuracy (Flow 3) and relevance (Flow 4) are independent scores. Interfaces can gate on accuracy first, then rank by relevance.

## Incentives: stake, reputation, and competence filtering

The mechanism uses two kinds of capital: **financial stake** (transferable) and **reputation** (non-transferable, topic-scoped, accumulated from accuracy). Vote weight: $w_i = s_i + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{rep}_i$ with caps and decay, where $\alpha$ is a pool parameter. When $\alpha = 0$, only stake matters and cash-poor experts have no influence; as $\alpha$ increases, reputation lowers the barrier but increases sensitivity to gaming. Decay bounds maximum influence of historical accuracy. The relevance game also produces a **competence filter**: incoherent participants lose stake and exit.

## Governance and UX: protocol vs interface

The design minimizes governance surface area to parameter updates and policy templates. **Interface capture** is mitigated by separating the censorship-resistant protocol (on-chain claims, stakes, verdicts) from opinionated interfaces (compliance, taste, safety filters). Alternative interfaces can independently index the same on-chain record.

## Funding: advertiser staking (bonded product claims)^[We avoid the term "proof of truth" because the protocol does not prove truth; it produces a stake-weighted, contestable signal.]

One funding path treats commercial claims as stakable assertions. An advertiser structures a product claim, posts stake, and either recovers it (true claim survives challenges, cost approaches zero) or loses it to the challenger (false claim). This inverts the cost structure: honest advertisers pay nearly nothing while dishonest advertisers bear the full cost. Digital advertising loses an estimated 20-30% of spend to fraud [@juniperresearch2023adfraud]; advertiser staking provides continuous verification demand even when news disputes are quiet.

# Truth Post: a partial instantiation {#sec-truthpost}

Truth Post (truthpost.news) launched in 2023 as a minimal implementation of the accuracy layer only, intended to validate the submission-and-challenge flow. It implemented author submission with staked bounties and challenger disputes routed to Kleros. The deployment omitted all protocol components beyond the accuracy layer: relevance curation (the coherence game), treasury rewards, confidence scores, pooled staking, and interface redundancy.

The deployment failed. Activity was sparse: fewer than 10 claims submitted, fewer than 5 challenges filed over approximately six months. The frontend stopped loading due to a subgraph indexing failure. The project was abandoned due to maintenance overhead and lack of investor interest.

Three lessons directly inform the full design. **The cold-start problem is real**: without critical mass, the system lacked economic activity to generate meaningful confidence signals, motivating pooled staking (Flow 2) and the confidence score design (Flow 1). **Relevance curation may be the engagement driver**: accuracy alone generated insufficient activity; the relevance layer (Flow 4) may be necessary for bootstrapping because people visit platforms to find what is important, not to verify boring truths. **Protocol/interface separation is a survival requirement**: a single frontend with a single subgraph dependency was a single point of failure, motivating the protocol-vs-interface separation principle.

# Related work

This work sits at the intersection of incentive design, oracle/dispute mechanisms, and information quality.

**Mechanism design for public goods.** @groves1977freeriderproblem solved the classical free rider problem [@samuelson1954publicgoods] by constructing mechanisms where each agent's tax includes a penalty proportional to how much their reported valuation deviates from the mean of others' reports, making truthful preference revelation a Nash equilibrium. Curated knowledge on a permissionless protocol is a public good (non-rivalrous, non-excludable), so the classical undersupply prediction applies.

This protocol applies two Groves-Ledyard insights: (1) the *deviation penalty* — the coherence game slashes curators whose ratings fall outside $K\sigma$ of the weighted mean, paralleling the Groves-Ledyard tax; (2) the *truth-telling incentive* — honest assessment is the focal equilibrium because deviating increases slashing probability. Four structural differences limit the analogy: the coherence game includes each agent's own report in $\mu$ (creating whale-manipulation risk, mitigated by weight caps); curation operates over a high-dimensional claim space with ordinal preferences rather than cardinal preferences over a single good; the coherence game produces a stake-weighted signal rather than a Pareto-optimal allocation; and the binary slash/reward payoff changes strategic incentives relative to the continuous deviation cost in Groves-Ledyard.^[Specifically: (1) Groves-Ledyard exclude each agent's own report from the penalty mean; (2) they assume cardinal preferences over a single public good; (3) both Welfare Theorems hold in their setting but not here; (4) their agents minimize a continuous cost function rather than optimizing to fall within a coherence band.]

**Token-curated registries (TCRs).** TCRs propose token-incentivized curation of lists [@goldin2017tcr]. We generalize the unit from "is item in list?" to claims + evidence + disputes, and separate accuracy from relevance.

**Decentralized dispute resolution.** Systems like Kleros operationalize decentralized arbitration using commit-reveal voting, staking, and appeals [@kleros2019shortpaper; @kleros2024yellowpaper], rooted in focal-point coordination [@schelling1960strategy]. Real deployments surface a key failure mode: ambiguity in what is being resolved. This paper treats semantic precision as a first-class security constraint. Academic critique emphasizes that jurors are rewarded for *coordination*, not epistemic correctness directly [@bergolla2022kleros; @kleros2021cryptoeconomics; @rojoarjona2021focalpoints].

**Escalation-based oracle resolution.** Reality.eth [@realityeth2023] implements crowd-sourced oracles using bond escalation, but operates at single-question granularity without curation-layer concerns (multi-dimensional quality, relevance scoring, evidence policies). The bond-escalation pattern informs Flow 3.

**Prediction markets and futarchy.** Prediction markets aggregate information via trading on future events [@hanson2013futarchy]. Our work differs in scope: curation operates over a high-dimensional claim space using staking and disputes rather than continuous trading. Resolution ambiguity in prediction markets (e.g., Augur, Polymarket) motivates our emphasis on claim templates.

**Peer prediction and BTS.** Peer prediction elicits information when ground truth is unavailable [@miller2005peerprediction]. @prelec2004bts proposed BTS, rewarding "surprisingly common" responses. A systematic comparison between BTS and the coherence game is an open direction.

**Commons governance.** @ostrom1990commons identified design principles for commons institutions (defined boundaries, graduated sanctions, low-cost conflict resolution, monitoring). This protocol has structural parallels but operates over a pseudonymous, adversarial participant base where identity is cheap and exit costless.

**Formalization gaps.** @george2023strategic proves an impossibility theorem for Schelling games with three or more ranked alternatives and formalizes the griefing factor framework [@george2023griefing]. @ast2023decentralized identifies the formalization gap as a recurring criticism. Our formal model responds: we cite the impossibility to bound our claims, use the griefing factor to quantify attack costs, and provide restricted-condition proofs where the impossibility does not bind.

**Data quality and TCR failures.** @wang1996beyondaccuracy emphasizes multi-dimensional, context-dependent quality; we adopt this to separate accuracy from relevance. TCR analyses surface equilibria where challenges are rare and participation decays [@asgaonkar2018tcrgametheory; @wang2019enhancing].

# Threat model and security analysis

## Threat model

We assume adversaries can be rational, coordinated, well-funded, and persistent. We target:

- Economic attacks: rich liars, collusion/bribery, low-stake spam, free riding.
- Game-theoretic attacks: lazy majorities, herding, consensus-over-correctness.
- Social/legal attacks: chilling effects, toxic content, interface capture.
- Epistemic attacks: ambiguity/context collapse, temporal decay.

Out of scope: breaking cryptography, coercion at gunpoint, and global-scale censorship of all clients.

## Stress tests (attack mapping)

@tbl-attack-defense summarizes the principal attacks and their defenses. A full attack-defense log with detailed narratives is maintained in the project repository.

| # | Attack | Defense | Mechanism reference |
|---|--------|---------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Lazy majority**: curators copy the majority vote without checking facts | Commit-reveal voting prevents copying; diligent challengers punish rubber-stamping by seizing stake | Flow 3 (challenge/dispute) |
| 2 | **Echo chambers**: biased pools curate lies under a permissive policy | Global accuracy is enforced cross-pool via DDR; pools control relevance policy but not accuracy verdicts | Separation of powers |
| 3 | **Liquidity crisis**: low-stakes lies survive because no one bothers to challenge | Low stake = low confidence score; unchallenged low-stake claims are treated as noise, not validation | Flow 1 (confidence signaling) |
| 4 | **Oracle capture (51% attack)**: adversary buys majority of DDR tokens | Economically suicidal (slippage + token collapse); community can fork to a new token | Trust assumptions; forking |
| 5 | **Wealth concentration**: competent curators accumulate all capital | Reputation as non-transferable capital lowers barrier for cash-poor experts; weight caps limit plutocracy | Incentives (stake + reputation) |
| 6 | **Chilling effect (liability)**: staking on truth exposes curators to lawsuits | Pooled staking + random drafting creates "herd immunity" against targeted liability | Flow 2 (pooled staking) |
| 7 | **Interface capture (meta-curation)**: dominant interface re-centralizes control | Protocol stores all claims/verdicts on-chain; alternative interfaces can independently index the same record | Governance and UX |
| 8 | **Deflationary spiral**: no disputes in peacetime, curators leave | Advertiser staking provides continuous verification demand even when political disputes are quiet | Funding (advertiser staking) |
| 9 | **Context collapse**: technically true but misleadingly vague claims | Vagueness = Rejection; under-specified claims are slashed, not forced into True/False | Claim templates |
| 10 | **Sybil flooding**: adversary creates many identities to overwhelm voting | Stake-weighted voting makes Sybil multiplication expensive; reputation is slow to build and non-transferable | Incentives; pooled staking |
| 11 | **Oracle manipulation (bribery)**: off-chain payments to jurors for desired verdicts | Commit-reveal + randomized juror selection + stake sizing that makes bribery uneconomical; acknowledged as incomplete defense | Flow 3; Limitations |
| 12 | **Temporal decay**: stale claims persist as "validated" long after truth changes | Stale claims become profitable challenge targets; authors are incentivized to withdraw obsolete claims; opt-in TTL field and automated $C$ decay (see Limitations) | Confidence signaling; challenge economics |
| 13 | **Pool governance capture**: coordinated bloc acquires majority governance tokens for a pool and rewrites curation policy to favor insiders | Forking as safety valve (any participant can create a competing pool); cross-pool competition degrades captured pools' signal quality; protocol-level parameter limits constrain governance surface area | Governance; curation policy bootstrap |
| 14 | **Temporal sniping**: adversary monitors claims nearing expiry (high $C$, stale evidence) and files last-second challenges when defenders have left | TTL field makes expiration explicit; automated $C$ decay reduces value of stale high-$C$ claims; challenge windows can require minimum remaining TTL | Temporal decay; Flow 3 |
| 15 | **Reputation laundering**: adversary builds reputation through honest participation in low-stakes rounds, then uses accumulated weight for a coordinated high-stakes attack | Reputation decay bounds maximum accumulated influence; topic-scoping prevents cross-domain reputation transfer; E4b quantifies the decay rate needed to contain this attack | Incentives; E4b |

: Principal attacks, defenses, and mechanism references. {#tbl-attack-defense}

# Evaluation

{{< include analysis/out/eval_summary.md >}}

## Research questions

- **RQ1 (dispute economics):** Under what parameter regimes is it rational to challenge false claims, and how does that affect false-claim survival?
- **RQ1a (adversarial persistence):** Is the dispute mechanism punitive at scale?
- **RQ2 (relevance robustness):** How robust is the coherence game to noisy curators and the threshold $K$?
- **RQ2a (collusion resistance):** At what colluding fraction does the coherence game break?
- **RQ3 (ambiguity defense):** Does Under-specified reduce wrong outcomes on ambiguous claims?
- **RQ4 (reputation mechanism):** At what $\alpha$ and $\delta$ does reputation accelerate expert entry vs create gaming vectors?

## E1: accuracy dispute simulation

We simulate a stream of claims (true/false), challengers who challenge when EV is positive, and juries with per-juror correctness $p$. We sweep bounty $B$, challenge stake $S$, jury size $N$, and juror accuracy $p$. Challenger EV is positive whenever $p > 0.50$ for all $S/B \le 0.50$ (@fig-e1-ev, @fig-e1-survival). For the $S/B$ ratios tested (0.05 to 0.50) with $N = 5$, the break-even threshold falls below $p = 0.50$. The binding constraint is the Condorcet condition: $p > 0.50$. The system becomes strongly self-enforcing at $p \ge 0.65$.

![E1: Challenger expected value (EV) on false claims as juror accuracy varies, for four stake-to-bounty ratios ($S/B$). $N = 5$ jurors, $p_{\text{detect}} = 0.35$. Higher $S/B$ ratios require higher juror accuracy for positive EV, but at $p \geq 0.65$ all tested ratios yield positive challenger EV, confirming that challenging false claims is rational across a wide parameter range.](analysis/fig/e1_challenger_ev.png){#fig-e1-ev}

![E1: False-claim survival probability after a single challenge window ($S/B = 0.25$, $N = 5$ jurors). As juror accuracy increases, the probability that a false claim survives a single detection-and-adjudication window decreases. At $p = 0.80$, survival probability is approximately 0.67, reflecting the combined effect of detection probability ($p_{\text{detect}} = 0.35$) and jury accuracy.](analysis/fig/e1_false_survival.png){#fig-e1-survival}

## E1-Adv: repeated attack by a well-funded adversary

E1 models individual challenges; E1-Adv tests what happens when a well-funded adversary submits 50 false claims simultaneously. For each claim, the adversary either goes undetected (probability $1 - p_{\text{detect}}$) or is challenged and faces a jury. Even at $p = 0.60$, the adversary's cumulative balance is deeply negative. At $p = 0.80$: $-1{,}638 \pm 68$ (95% CI, $N = 100$ seeds), approximately $33\times$ bounty loss. At $p = 0.90$: $-1{,}749 \pm 71$. Unchallenged claims survive but accumulate minimal confidence (@fig-e1-adv).

![E1-Adv: Survival rate and adversary profit/loss across 50 repeated false-claim attacks. Error bars show 95% CI over $N = 100$ independent seeds. At all jury accuracy levels tested ($p = 0.60$ to $0.90$), the adversary's cumulative balance is deeply negative, confirming that volume attacks are economically punitive.](analysis/fig/e1_adversarial.png){#fig-e1-adv}

## E2: relevance coherence game

We simulate $M$ curators with evolving weights playing repeated relevance rounds on items with ground-truth relevance $r \in [0,1]$. Competent curators vote $r + \epsilon$ (noise); incompetent curators vote uniformly at random. We sweep fraction of competent curators, noise level, coherence threshold $K$, and number of rounds. Higher competent fractions produce lower error at all $K$ values; tighter thresholds ($K = 0.8$) produce lower error when competent curators dominate but are less forgiving of honest noise (@fig-e2-error). Even from 10% initial competence, the coherence game concentrates stake among competent participants; at 50%+ initial competence, final competent stake share exceeds 0.95 (@fig-e2-filter).

![E2: Mean relevance error ($|\mu - r|$) vs initial fraction of competent curators, for four coherence thresholds $K$. 200 curators, 200 rounds. Higher competent fractions produce lower error at all $K$ values. Tighter thresholds ($K = 0.8$) produce lower error when competent curators dominate but are less forgiving of honest noise.](analysis/fig/e2_relevance_error.png){#fig-e2-error}

![E2: Final competent stake share after 200 rounds of coherence filtering ($K = 1.25$). Even when starting with only 10% competent curators, the coherence game concentrates stake among competent participants. At 50% initial competence and above, final competent stake share exceeds 0.95.](analysis/fig/e2_competence_filter.png){#fig-e2-filter}

## E2-Adv: coherence game under adversarial collusion

A colluding bloc coordinates on biased ratings (shift +0.30). Colluders are *competent-with-bias* — they observe true relevance and systematically shift it, making them harder to eject than random voters. We sweep colluding fraction from 0% to 30% with 60% honest-competent curators and $K = 1.25$.

Two regimes emerge ($N = 100$ seeds, 95% CI). Below 20% collusion, the mechanism ejects colluders: signal error increases modestly ($0.037 \pm 0.000$ to $0.064 \pm 0.001$) and colluder stake decays to 2.5%. At 30%, the mechanism breaks: the bloc shifts $\mu$ toward their biased target, redefining the coherent band around themselves. Colluder stake share rises to $0.80 \pm 0.005$ and signal error reaches $0.144 \pm 0.001$ (@fig-e2-adv). The 20-30% boundary is a stable property of the mechanism, confirmed by tight confidence intervals.

![E2-Adv: Signal error and colluder stake share under coordinated manipulation. Shaded bands show 95% CI over $N = 100$ independent seeds. Below 20% collusion, signal error increases modestly and colluders are ejected. At 30%, the mechanism breaks: colluders redefine the coherent band and capture $\sim$80% of stake.](analysis/fig/e2_adversarial.png){#fig-e2-adv}

## E3: ambiguity stress test

We generate a mixture of well-posed and ambiguous claims. Baseline forces True/False even when ambiguous; the defended system allows Under-specified and penalizes ambiguity at submission. At 25% ambiguity prevalence, wrong-resolution rate drops from 0.12 to 0.02 (83% improvement, @fig-e3-ambiguity). The improvement scales with ambiguity prevalence: at 50% ambiguous claims, the defended system reduces errors by over 90%.

![E3: Overall wrong-resolution rate as ambiguity prevalence increases. Baseline forces True/False on all claims; defended allows Under-specified. At 25% ambiguity, the defended system reduces wrong-resolution rate from 0.12 to 0.02 (83% improvement).](analysis/fig/e3_ambiguity.png){#fig-e3-ambiguity}

## E4: reputation mechanism validation

E4 addresses reputation ($w_i = s_i + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{rep}_i$ with decay $\delta$) with three sub-experiments ($N = 100$ seeds each).

**E4a: Alpha and decay sweep.** We extend the E2 coherence game (200 curators, $K = 1.25$) to 500 rounds with reputation enabled, sweeping $\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0\}$ and $\delta \in \{0.0, 0.01, 0.05\}$, including "cash-poor expert" agents who start with $s_i = 0.1$ (vs median 1.0) but are competent. At $\alpha = 0$, cash-poor experts need ~137 rounds to reach median weight (Gini $\approx 0.61$). At $\alpha = 0.5$, $\delta = 0.01$: time-to-entry drops to 8 rounds, Gini falls to 0.17, but mean error increases from 0.027 to 0.088 because reputation accumulates for any coherent curator, including those coherent by luck. Higher decay rates moderate this: at $\delta = 0.05$, error at $\alpha = 0.5$ is 0.079. Deployment guidance: expert-inclusion pools should target $\alpha \in [0.25, 0.50]$ with $\delta \geq 0.05$ (~$3\times$ worse error for ~$17\times$ faster entry); signal-fidelity pools should use $\alpha \leq 0.10$. The decay rate $\delta$ dominates $\alpha$ in controlling gaming persistence (@fig-e4a-heatmap, @fig-e4a-gini).

![E4a: Rounds until cash-poor expert reaches median weight, as a function of reputation weight $\alpha$ and decay rate $\delta$. Lower values (lighter colors) indicate faster entry. At $\alpha = 0$ (no reputation), cash-poor experts require $\sim$137 rounds; at $\alpha \geq 0.25$, entry occurs within 8-20 rounds.](analysis/fig/e4a_alpha_heatmap.png){#fig-e4a-heatmap}

![E4a: Gini coefficient of final weight distribution vs $\alpha$ for each decay rate. Error bars show 95% CI over $N = 100$ seeds. Reputation ($\alpha > 0$) substantially reduces weight inequality.](analysis/fig/e4a_gini.png){#fig-e4a-gini}

**E4b: Reputation gaming.** A strategic attacker starts with $\mathrm{rep}_0 = 200$ (equivalent to 200 rounds of coherent voting) but now votes randomly. Without decay ($\delta = 0$): permanent entrenchment (all 300 rounds above-median). At $\delta = 0.05$: ~61 rounds ($\pm 1$, 95% CI). At $\delta = 0.10$: ~36 rounds. The decay rate dominates ($< 5$ rounds difference across $\alpha$ values at any given $\delta$). Any deployment with $\alpha > 0$ must use $\delta > 0$ (@fig-e4b-gaming).

![E4b: Rounds (of 300) that a reputation-rich attacker retains above-median weight, as a function of decay rate and $\alpha$. Error bars show 95% CI. Without decay ($\delta = 0$), the attacker dominates indefinitely. At $\delta \geq 0.05$, influence is bounded to $\sim$60 rounds regardless of $\alpha$.](analysis/fig/e4b_gaming_decay.png){#fig-e4b-gaming}

**E4c: Sybil laundering.** Twenty Sybil identities vote coherently for 100 rounds to accumulate reputation, then coordinate a biased attack for 100 rounds. At $\alpha = 0$: attack-phase error is 0.023, Sybil weight share 0.014 (no advantage). At $\alpha = 0.5$: error rises to 0.072 ($\pm 0.001$, 95% CI), Sybil weight share reaches 0.092. Reputation makes Sybil laundering more effective, not less; defense is decay + topic-scoping (@fig-e4c-sybil).

![E4c: Signal error during Sybil attack phase (left) and final Sybil weight share (right) as a function of $\alpha$. At $\alpha = 0$, Sybil buildup has no advantage; at $\alpha > 0$, accumulated reputation amplifies the attack. Gray dashed line shows initial Sybil population share.](analysis/fig/e4c_sybil_comparison.png){#fig-e4c-sybil}

## Reproducibility

All simulations are deterministic (fixed RNG seeds) and run in CI on every commit. Adversarial experiments and E4 use $N = 100$ seeds with reported means and 95% confidence intervals.

# Limitations and open problems

## Limited deployment evidence

No live deployment of the full protocol exists. Truth Post (2023) tested the accuracy layer only and did not achieve sustained usage (see @sec-truthpost). All claims about incentive alignment and competence filtering are conditional on parameters swept in simulation only.

## Signal limitations

The protocol produces **stake-weighted, contestable labels**, not knowledge. The system can converge on wrong equilibria when evidence is ambiguous, participants are lazy, or incentives are mis-set [@bergolla2022kleros; @kleros2021cryptoeconomics]. Coordination on "what others will vote" can diverge from correctness, especially with expertise requirements or conflicts of interest [@rojoarjona2021focalpoints].

## Independence and bribery

The challenger EV formula assumes independent juror votes. In practice, herding, shared information sources, and off-chain coordination introduce correlation, reducing effective jury size. Commit-reveal reduces copying but does not prevent off-chain coordination or delayed bribes [@consensysPlcrVoting; @consensysDiligenceTcrAudit].

## Cold start and deployment bootstrap

The mechanism requires simultaneous bootstrapping of authors, validators, challengers, and readers — a chicken-and-egg problem that is particularly acute because the value proposition depends on stake liquidity and dispute activity.

**Strategy 1: Seeded single-domain launch.** Launch with one narrow domain where a founding cohort of 10-20 participants can generate meaningful coverage, a known external dataset provides ground truth, and the evidence policy is unambiguous. Risk: too niche → no organic growth; too broad → quality collapses before sufficient stake liquidity.

**Strategy 2: Retroactive validation.** Import existing public claims as unclaimed entries with zero bounty; anyone adopts by posting stake. This requires a claim adoption protocol (template conformance, provenance tracking, adoption stake sizing) flagged as a pre-deployment deliverable.

Both strategies require subsidized participation during the bootstrap phase; neither is validated.

## Scalability and UX friction

On-chain operations create gas cost and throughput limitations for low-value claims. Staking, structured claim authoring, and dispute participation impose cognitive and financial costs that may limit adoption to specialists.

## Governance and sustainability

Token-weighted governance can plutocratize. Forking is a social process with legitimacy disputes, not an automatic guarantee. Verified truth is a public good; sustainability may require mixed funding models.

## Domain expertise

Hard domains (law, medicine, finance) require credible expertise signals. Pooled staking and reputation help but do not replace expert institutions.

## Reputation mechanism: validated with tradeoffs

E4 confirms a quantifiable equity-accuracy tradeoff: at $\alpha = 0.5$, cash-poor experts reach median weight in ~8 rounds (vs 137 at $\alpha = 0$), but error increases from 0.027 to 0.088. Reputation gaming is bounded by decay ($\delta \geq 0.05$). Sybil laundering is amplified by reputation ($\alpha > 0$), confirming that topic-scoping and decay are necessary complements.

## Formal model limitations

Three limitations concern gaps in the formal model. First, **curation policy authoring remains a governance problem**: the focal point equilibrium (Proposition 2) is conditional on curation policies being specific enough to induce a unique coordination target; whether community governance reliably produces such policies, particularly in hard domains (medicine, law, climate), is an open empirical question. Second, **focal-point uniqueness is assumed, not proven**: the coherence game's equilibrium depends on the curation policy inducing a unique focal point, but this is a design heuristic validated under the simulation's ground-truth relevance model, not a formal theorem; multi-modal interpretation distributions are possible in deployed pools with diverse curator backgrounds, and we treat high $\sigma$ as a measurable failure signal rather than a provable guarantee (see the focal-point discussion in the Mechanisms section). Third, **smart contract attack surfaces**: deployment requires smart contract implementations of staking, slashing, commit-reveal, and payout logic, which are attack surfaces for reentrancy, integer overflow, front-running (MEV), and storage manipulation. A production deployment requires formal verification, independent security audit, time-locked upgradability, and a bug bounty program. Core accounting invariants that must hold: (1) stake conservation, (2) slash boundedness (no negative balances), (3) commit-reveal integrity, (4) payout exclusivity, (5) cooldown monotonicity, and (6) confidence monotonicity.

## Temporal decay

Claims become stale. Two mechanisms address this: opt-in TTL (time-to-live) in claim templates, and automated confidence decay $C = \sum_t B_t \cdot \Delta t \cdot e^{-\lambda(T_{\text{now}} - t)}$ where $\lambda$ is a pool-specific governance parameter.

## Simulation limitations

E1-Adv, E2-Adv, and E4 use $N = 100$ independent seeds with reported means and 95% confidence intervals. Directional results are robust; specific magnitudes should be interpreted within reported intervals.

# Conclusion

The core claim: the bottleneck behind most coordination failures is not governance or voting but the upstream transformation of information into knowledge. We propose a four-step framework for trustless curation (problem definition, use case selection, quality identification, mechanism design) and instantiate it for news, separating accuracy (binary, evidence-based, dispute-resolved) from relevance (non-binary, policy-guided, coherence-game-resolved).

Simulations show that challengers have positive EV against false claims when $p > 0.50$, the coherence game filters incompetent participants, and Under-specified substantially reduces wrong resolutions. Adversarial simulations confirm the dispute mechanism is economically punitive ($-1{,}638 \pm 68$ per 50 false claims at $p = 0.80$) and the coherence game ejects colluding minorities but breaks above ~20-30% of stake. The reputation mechanism introduces a quantifiable equity-accuracy tradeoff: at $\alpha = 0.5$, cash-poor experts reach parity in ~8 rounds (vs 137 without reputation), but signal error increases from 0.027 to 0.088. Reputation gaming is bounded by decay ($\delta \geq 0.05$), but Sybil laundering is amplified ($\alpha > 0$), confirming that decay and topic-scoping are necessary complements.

The design depends on assumptions untested in deployment: that stake sizes will attract competent participation, that dispute resolution produces accurate verdicts at acceptable cost, that claim templates can be made precise enough without becoming expert gatekeepers, that the cold-start problem can be overcome, and that the focal-point uniqueness assumption holds in diverse curator pools. The most important open problems are deployment evidence, UX friction, and the sustainability of curation as a public good.

# Disclosure

The author has multi-year engineering experience with Kleros, a deployed decentralized dispute resolution system. This experience informs the design choices and threat model but does not constitute empirical validation. No deployment data from Kleros is used in this paper. The author does not hold PNK tokens and has no ongoing financial relationship with Kleros.
